title: Demonstrate basic understanding of the Primary labour legislation that impacts on a business unit

lessons.title: The labour laws that regulate employment
lessons.html:
Why a supervisor must know labour law

Team leaders, supervisors and section heads in farms, packhouses and abattoirs make daily decisions about hours, leave, discipline and hiring. These decisions must comply with labour law. Mistakes can lead to disputes at the CCMA (Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration), compensation orders, fines and damaged working relationships.

The primary labour laws

ActMain purpose
Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996Right to fair labour practices, to form and join trade unions, and to strike
Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 (LRA)Collective bargaining, unions, dispute resolution, fair dismissal, unfair labour practices
Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997 (BCEA)Minimum conditions: hours, overtime, leave, notice, records
Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998 (EEA)Prohibits unfair discrimination; affirmative action by designated employers
Skills Development Act 97 of 1998 (SDA)Develops workforce skills through SETAs, learnerships and workplace skills plans
Skills Development Levies Act 9 of 1999 (SDLA)Funds skills development through a payroll levy
Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993Safe and healthy workplaces
Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act 130 of 1993Compensation for work injuries and diseases
Unemployment Insurance Act 63 of 2001UIF benefits for unemployment, illness, maternity
National Minimum Wage Act 9 of 2018Sets the national minimum wage

For agriculture, the Sectoral Determination for the Farm Worker Sector made under the BCEA sets specific conditions for farm workers. Supervisors must know which sectoral determination or bargaining council agreement applies to their workplace.

lessons.title: The Labour Relations Act and interviews
lessons.html:
Main aspects of the LRA

  • Freedom of association: employees may join trade unions and take part in lawful union activities. Employees and job seekers may not be victimised for this.
  • Organisational rights: sufficiently representative unions may get access to the workplace, stop-order deductions of subscriptions, and recognition of shop stewards.
  • Collective bargaining: through bargaining councils or agreements between employers and unions.
  • Strikes and lock-outs: protected if the LRA's procedures are followed.
  • Workplace forums for consultation in larger workplaces.
  • Dispute resolution: through the CCMA, bargaining councils and the Labour Court.
  • Unfair dismissal and unfair labour practices: dismissals must be substantively fair (a fair reason: misconduct, incapacity or operational requirements) and procedurally fair (a fair process). The Code of Good Practice: Dismissal guides employers.

A fair disciplinary process in practice

  1. Investigate the facts.
  2. Inform the employee of the allegation in a language they understand.
  3. Give reasonable time to prepare and allow representation by a co-worker or shop steward.
  4. Hold a hearing where the employee can respond.
  5. Decide on a fair sanction, considering the rule, consistency and the employee's record.
  6. Inform the employee of the outcome and their right to refer a dispute.

Interviews and recruitment

Job seekers are protected by labour law. When interviewing:

  • Do not ask about union membership or union activities.
  • Do not ask questions that may lead to unfair discrimination, such as pregnancy plans, religion, HIV status, marital status or family responsibilities, unless directly linked to an inherent job requirement and permitted by law.
  • Use the same job-related questions for all candidates and record answers.
  • Base decisions on the job requirements, skills and experience.

lessons.title: The Basic Conditions of Employment Act
lessons.html:
Minimum conditions

The BCEA sets the minimum conditions of employment. Contracts, collective agreements and sectoral determinations may give better conditions but, in general, not worse. Some provisions do not apply to senior managers or employees earning above the earnings threshold set by the Minister.

Key provisions

TopicBasic rule
Ordinary hoursA maximum of 45 hours a week
OvertimeOnly by agreement; limited to 10 hours a week; paid at one and a half times the normal rate, or time off by agreement
Meal intervalA meal interval after 5 hours of continuous work
Daily and weekly restMinimum rest periods between shifts and each week
Sunday and public holiday workHigher pay rates unless agreed otherwise within the Act
Annual leave21 consecutive days per annual leave cycle (or by agreement 1 day for every 17 days worked)
Sick leaveOver a 36-month cycle, paid sick leave equal to the days normally worked in six weeks
Maternity leaveAt least four consecutive months
Family responsibility leave3 days per year for qualifying events
NoticeDepends on length of service
Written particulars and payslipsEmployees must receive written particulars of employment and a payslip with each payment

The Act also prohibits child labour and forced labour. Employers must keep records of time worked and remuneration.

Supervisor's role

  • Plan rosters within the hour limits, including during harvest peaks.
  • Record overtime accurately and get agreement for it.
  • Handle leave requests fairly and keep records.
  • Check the sectoral determination for farm workers, which may have specific rules.

lessons.title: Employment equity and skills development
lessons.html:
Employment Equity Act

The EEA has two main parts:

  1. Prohibition of unfair discrimination applies to all employers. No one may unfairly discriminate against an employee or job applicant on grounds such as race, gender, sex, pregnancy, marital status, family responsibility, ethnic or social origin, colour, sexual orientation, age, disability, religion, HIV status, conscience, belief, political opinion, culture, language or birth. Equal pay for work of equal value is required.
  2. Affirmative action applies to designated employers, such as employers with 50 or more employees and certain others defined in the Act. They must consult employees, analyse their workforce, prepare an employment equity plan and submit reports to the Department of Employment and Labour. Designated groups are black people (Africans, Coloureds and Indians), women and people with disabilities.

A supervisor supports the plan by fair recruitment and promotion, reasonable accommodation of people with disabilities, and acting against harassment.

Skills Development Act and Skills Development Levies Act

  • SETAs (Sector Education and Training Authorities) manage skills development in each sector. Agriculture falls under the AgriSETA.
  • Employers appoint a skills development facilitator and submit a workplace skills plan and annual training report to their SETA to claim grants.
  • Learnerships and skills programmes lead to registered qualifications.
  • The skills development levy is 1% of the payroll, paid monthly to SARS by employers whose annual payroll exceeds the threshold (currently R500 000). Part of the levy returns to employers as grants when they train.

Supervisor's role in skills

Identify training needs in your team, release workers for training, mentor learners on the job, and keep records of training completed.

Key points

  • The LRA governs unions, collective bargaining, disputes and fair dismissal.
  • Interview questions must be job-related and must not lead to unfair discrimination.
  • The BCEA sets minimum conditions: 45 ordinary hours a week, overtime limits, leave and payslips.
  • The EEA prohibits unfair discrimination and requires designated employers to implement affirmative action.
  • The SDA and SDLA fund training through SETAs, such as the AgriSETA, using a 1% payroll levy.
